data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Herpes zoster** (Viral infections)_

**Q1. Define herpes zoster. What is its pathogenesis?**
- Reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus from a sensory (dorsal root or cranial nerve) ganglion, producing painful unilateral dermatomal vesicular eruption
- Fall in VZV-specific cell-mediated immunity with age (>50 y), HIV, malignancy (lymphoma), chemotherapy, steroids, JAK inhibitors, transplant, stress, trauma
- Virus travels down the sensory nerve to skin; ganglionitis causes pain

**Q2. Which dermatomes are commonly affected?**
- Thoracic (T3–L2) commonest (~50%), then trigeminal (ophthalmic division), cervical, lumbosacral
- Usually one dermatome; may involve adjacent ones; crosses midline only slightly

**Q3. Describe the clinical course.**
- Prodrome 1–5 days: burning, itching, pain (may mimic angina, cholecystitis, renal colic), fever, malaise
- Erythematous papules → grouped vesicles in a band along the dermatome → pustules → crusts by 7–10 days; heals in 2–4 weeks
- Zoster sine herpete: pain without rash
- Few vesicles (<20) outside the dermatome are allowed; more suggests dissemination

**Q4. What is disseminated zoster?**
- More than 20 vesicles outside the primary and adjacent dermatomes, or ≥3 dermatomes involved, or visceral involvement — implies immunosuppression (HIV, malignancy); needs IV acyclovir

**Q5. What is herpes zoster ophthalmicus and Hutchinson's sign?**
- Zoster of the ophthalmic division of trigeminal nerve (V1)
- Hutchinson's sign: vesicles on the tip/side of nose (external nasal branch of nasociliary nerve) — high risk of eye involvement (keratitis, uveitis, glaucoma, retinitis, optic neuritis)
- Needs ophthalmology referral and systemic antivirals

**Q6. What is Ramsay Hunt syndrome?**
- Zoster of geniculate ganglion of facial nerve — ipsilateral lower motor neurone facial palsy, ear pain, vesicles on the ear (concha, external canal), taste loss in anterior 2/3 of tongue, tinnitus, vertigo, hearing loss
- Worse recovery than Bell's palsy — antivirals + prednisolone early

**Q7. Name other complications.**
- Post-herpetic neuralgia (commonest)
- Secondary bacterial infection, scarring, pigmentation, Koebner (granulomatous/ lichenoid lesions at healed sites — Wolf's isotopic response)
- Motor palsy (e.g. foot drop, bladder dysfunction in sacral zoster, abdominal wall pseudohernia)
- Meningoencephalitis, myelitis, Guillain–Barré, stroke (VZV vasculopathy — granulomatous arteritis), pneumonitis, hepatitis

**Q8. Define post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) and its risk factors. (short note)**
- Pain persisting ≥90 days (3 months) after rash onset (some use 1 month)
- Risk: older age (>50), severe prodromal pain, severe acute pain, extensive rash, ophthalmic involvement, immunosuppression, diabetes, delayed antiviral therapy
- Pain types: burning, lancinating, allodynia (pain to light touch — very characteristic)

**Q9. Management of PHN.**
- First line: pregabalin (75–300 mg twice daily) or gabapentin (titrate to 1800–3600 mg/day); tricyclics — amitriptyline/nortriptyline 10–75 mg at night
- Topical: lidocaine 5% patch, capsaicin 0.075% cream or 8% patch
- Second line: tramadol, opioids; duloxetine; nerve blocks; TENS
- Prevention: early antiviral, adequate acute pain control, vaccination

**Q10. How do you treat acute zoster?**
- Antivirals ideally within 72 h of rash onset (later if new vesicles still forming, ophthalmic, immunosuppressed): acyclovir 800 mg five times daily × 7 days; valacyclovir 1 g thrice daily × 7 days; famciclovir 500 mg thrice daily × 7 days
- IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly for disseminated/immunocompromised/CNS involvement
- Adjust dose for renal function
- Analgesics (paracetamol/NSAIDs, pregabalin for severe acute pain), calamine, wet compresses, antibiotics for secondary infection
- Systemic steroids do not prevent PHN — only for Ramsay Hunt/ocular inflammation under supervision

**Q11. What is the Tzanck smear and PCR role?**
- Tzanck — multinucleated giant cells; cannot differentiate HSV vs VZV
- PCR of vesicle fluid is the test of choice for atypical or zoster sine herpete (PCR on CSF/blood)

**Q12. Differentiate herpes zoster from zosteriform herpes simplex.**
- HSV: recurrent at the same site, smaller grouped vesicles, less pain, no PHN, younger patients
- Zoster: usually once (recurrence in ~5%), dermatomal band, severe pain, older age, PHN risk
- PCR settles it

**Q13. Differential diagnosis of herpes zoster.**
- Zosteriform HSV, contact dermatitis (linear plant contact), bullous impetigo, insect bites, fixed drug eruption, linear lichen planus/porokeratosis (chronic, no pain)
- Prodrome mimics: myocardial infarction, renal colic, appendicitis, migraine

**Q14. What are zosteriform lesions? (asked in PYQ)**
- Lesions arranged in a band along a dermatome but not due to VZV — zosteriform herpes simplex, zosteriform metastases (breast cancer), zosteriform lichen planus, segmental vitiligo, zosteriform naevi, segmental neurofibromatosis, zosteriform leiomyomas
- Contrast with blaschkoid (follow Blaschko's lines — mosaic genetic disorders)

**Q15. Why should you test for HIV in zoster?**
- Zoster in a young adult (<50 y), multi-dermatomal, recurrent, disseminated, necrotic/chronic verrucous lesions may be the first sign of HIV — offer HIV test

**Q16. Zoster vaccines?**
- Recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV, Shingrix — gE glycoprotein + AS01B adjuvant): 2 doses IM 2–6 months apart; ≥50 years and ≥18 years if immunocompromised; ~90% efficacy; non-live, safe in immunocompromised (available in India since 2023)
- Live attenuated zoster vaccine (Zostavax) — discontinued in many countries; contraindicated in immunosuppression
- Reduces zoster and PHN

**Q17. Is zoster contagious?**
- Yes — vesicle fluid can give chickenpox (not zoster) to non-immune people; cover lesions; airborne precautions for disseminated zoster or immunocompromised patients

**Q18. Zoster in pregnancy?**
- Fetal risk is minimal (maternal antibodies present); treat mother with acyclovir if needed

## Quick spotter facts
- Unilateral dermatomal grouped vesicles with pain — zoster
- Hutchinson's sign — nasal tip vesicles → eye involvement
- PHN = pain ≥90 days; allodynia

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Viral infections — VZV). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
